concepts.label: The ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of the thalamus receives the trigeminal lemniscus
concepts.article_title: VPM nucleus and the trigeminal lemniscus
concepts.definition: The trigeminal lemniscus (the combined trigeminothalamic pathway) carries pain, temperature and touch information from the face and oral cavity, relayed through the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei, crosses the midline in the pons and medulla, and ascends to terminate in the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus. VPM is the facial counterpart of the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus, which receives the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract carrying the equivalent modalities from the body. From VPM, third-order neurons project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the face representation of the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus as the destination of the trigeminal lemniscus.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing VPM (face sensation via the trigeminal lemniscus) with VPL (body sensation via the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract) — the two nuclei sit side by side in the thalamus and are functionally parallel, differing only in the body region relayed.
concepts.original_wording: Source Anatomy item 1 ("VPMN receives - Trigeminal lemniscus"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Anatomy item 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p1, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: The Papez circuit mediates the prolongation and elaboration of emotional experience
concepts.definition: The Papez circuit is a closed neural loop — hippocampus to fornix to mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nucleus via the mammillothalamic tract to the cingulate gyrus and back to the hippocampus via the cingulum — first proposed by James Papez as the anatomical substrate of emotion. Its principal physiological role is not to generate an emotional response from scratch (a task more dependent on the amygdala) but to sustain, elaborate and give lasting, consciously felt quality to an emotion once it has begun, binding it to memory. Lesions affecting circuit components, such as mammillary body damage in Korsakoff syndrome, disrupt this link between emotion and memory rather than abolishing emotional reactivity outright.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute prolongation and conscious elaboration of an ongoing emotional experience to the Papez circuit.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Limbic system and emotion
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the Papez circuit's role (prolonging and elaborating an emotion already underway, linking it to memory) with the amygdala's role (initiating the emotional response, particularly fear) — both are limbic structures but serve complementary rather than identical functions.
concepts.original_wording: Source Anatomy item 2 ("Papez circuit function - Prolonged emotions"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Anatomy item 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p1, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus
concepts.definition: The third pharyngeal pouch has dorsal and ventral wings: the dorsal wing forms the inferior parathyroid glands, and the ventral wing forms the thymus. The third-pouch parathyroid primordium migrates further caudally than the fourth pouch's does, so the inferior parathyroid glands end up more variable in final position and are occasionally pulled down with the descending thymus into the superior mediastinum, the classic explanation for ectopic mediastinal parathyroid tissue. Sharing a pouch of origin also explains why thymic and inferior parathyroid tissue are occasionally found together in developmental anomalies such as DiGeorge syndrome.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus to the third pharyngeal pouch.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the third pouch (inferior parathyroid + thymus) with the fourth pouch (superior parathyroid + ultimobranchial body/parafollicular C cells) — the third pouch's derivatives migrate further and end up positioned inferior to the fourth pouch's despite arising from a more cranial pouch, a common source of exam error.
concepts.original_wording: Source Anatomy item 3 ("Inferior parathyroid gland and thymus are derived from which pharyngeal pouch - 3rd"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Anatomy item 3 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p1, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: The rhombic lip of the metencephalon gives rise to the cerebellum
concepts.definition: The metencephalon, the rostral part of the embryonic hindbrain, gives rise to both the pons and the cerebellum. The cerebellum develops specifically from the rhombic lips, paired dorsolateral thickenings of the metencephalon's alar plate, which fuse in the midline over the roof of the fourth ventricle. Neuroblasts migrating from the rhombic lip form the cerebellar cortex and deep cerebellar nuclei, and, via a transient external germinal (granular) layer, give rise to the numerous granule cells characteristic of the mature cerebellum.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute the cerebellum's embryological origin to the rhombic lip of the metencephalon.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the rhombic lip (a metencephalic derivative that forms the cerebellum) with the alar plate of the myelencephalon (which forms the sensory nuclei of the medulla, not the cerebellum) — both are hindbrain alar-plate derivatives but give rise to different adult structures.
concepts.original_wording: Source Anatomy item 4 ("….is formed from rhombic lip of metencephalon - Cerebellum"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p1.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Anatomy item 4 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p1, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Recognition of faces is a function of the representational (non-dominant) cerebral hemisphere
concepts.definition: Cerebral hemispheric specialisation assigns language, calculation and sequential/analytic tasks chiefly to the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, while the non-dominant hemisphere — often termed the 'representational' hemisphere — specialises in visuospatial and holistic processing tasks, including facial recognition, spatial orientation, and musical/emotional prosody. Damage to the non-dominant parietal and temporal-occipital association cortex characteristically produces prosopagnosia (inability to recognise familiar faces) and other visuospatial deficits, even though language remains intact. This lateralisation is not absolute but reflects a strong statistical bias, particularly well documented in right-handed individuals whose left hemisphere is dominant for language.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute facial recognition to the representational (non-dominant) cerebral hemisphere.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the non-dominant hemisphere is functionally silent because it lacks language — it carries its own specialised repertoire (facial recognition, spatial processing, musical/emotional prosody), and its damage produces distinct deficits such as prosopagnosia rather than aphasia.
concepts.original_wording: Source Physio item 2 ("Recognition of faces - Representational hemisphere"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p1-2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Physio item 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p1-2, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Naming a seen object depends on a pathway from the visual cortex through Wernicke's area and Broca's area to the primary motor cortex
concepts.definition: Naming an object that has just been seen requires the primary visual cortex to pass the visual percept, via visual association areas and the angular gyrus, to Wernicke's area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, where the visual image is matched to its corresponding word. That word-formulation output travels via the arcuate fasciculus to Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus, which programs the sequence of articulatory movements, and finally to the primary motor cortex, which executes the movements of the lips, tongue and larynx via the corticobulbar tract. A lesion at any point along this chain produces a different, localisable deficit — from visual object agnosia to Wernicke's (receptive) or Broca's (expressive) aphasia to dysarthria.
concepts.explicit_objective: Sequence the pathway from seeing an object to naming it aloud: visual cortex, Wernicke's area, Broca's area, primary motor cortex.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Language and higher cortical function
aliases: Visual cortex to Wernicke's to Broca's pathway
concepts.pitfalls: Reversing the order of Wernicke's and Broca's areas in this pathway — comprehension/word-formulation (Wernicke's) precedes motor speech programming (Broca's), connected by the arcuate fasciculus; swapping them misattributes the resulting aphasia type to a lesion.
concepts.original_wording: Source Physio item 3 ("True Consequence for seeing object then speak - Visual cortex – Wernicke's area – Broca's area – primary motor area"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Physio item 3 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p2, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Flumazenil is the specific antidote for midazolam (benzodiazepine) overdose
concepts.definition: Midazolam, like other benzodiazepines, acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the GABA-A receptor, increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening in response to GABA. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor: it displaces midazolam and other benzodiazepines from the receptor without itself activating it, rapidly reversing sedation, respiratory depression and anaesthetic effects. Because flumazenil's half-life is shorter than that of most benzodiazepines, re-sedation can occur once it wears off, so patients require monitoring after reversal, and flumazenil can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify flumazenil as the receptor-competitive antidote that reverses midazolam and other benzodiazepine effects.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming flumazenil's reversal is permanent — its shorter half-life relative to most benzodiazepines means re-sedation can recur, and abrupt reversal risks precipitating seizures in a benzodiazepine-dependent patient.
concepts.original_wording: Source Pharma item 1 ("Midazolam antidote - Flumazenil"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Pharma item 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p2, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Amitriptyline is used for migraine prophylaxis and also improves insomnia, unlike propranolol
concepts.definition: Amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, is a first-line agent for migraine prophylaxis independent of its antidepressant action, likely via modulation of central serotonergic and noradrenergic pain-processing pathways. Its pronounced antihistaminic and anticholinergic sedative properties also make it useful for patients whose migraines are accompanied by insomnia, since the same dose that helps prevent headaches also improves sleep onset and quality. Propranolol, a beta-blocker, is another first-line migraine prophylactic agent, but it lacks amitriptyline's sedative, sleep-promoting effect and can itself cause sleep disturbance (vivid dreams, insomnia) in some patients, making amitriptyline the preferred choice when insomnia coexists with migraine.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify amitriptyline as a migraine-prophylactic agent that also improves insomnia, distinguishing it from propranolol.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming any migraine prophylactic agent also aids sleep — propranolol, another first-line option, does not share amitriptyline's sedative anticholinergic/antihistaminic profile and can worsen rather than improve sleep in some patients.
concepts.original_wording: Source Pharma item 2 ("…. Used for migraine prophylaxis and improve insomnia - Amitriptyline (Not propranolol)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Pharma item 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p2, answer/topic stated before the stem, with the source itself naming propranolol as the excluded distractor — this batch authors its own remaining distractors.

concepts.label: Rifampin for 2 days is used as chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of Neisseria meningitidis infection
concepts.definition: Close contacts of a patient with invasive Neisseria meningitidis infection are at markedly increased risk of secondary disease and require chemoprophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage, since the organism spreads by respiratory droplets. Rifampin, given orally for two days (typically every 12 hours), is one of the standard regimens for this purpose, alongside single-dose ciprofloxacin or intramuscular ceftriaxone; rifampin is preferred in some settings, such as young children, but colours body secretions orange and can reduce oral contraceptive efficacy through hepatic enzyme induction. Prophylaxis is intended for close contacts (household, healthcare workers with direct mucosal exposure) rather than the wider public, and should be given as soon as possible after exposure is identified.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify the 2-day rifampin regimen as a standard chemoprophylaxis option for close contacts of Neisseria meningitidis infection.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing chemoprophylaxis (short-course rifampin/ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone for close contacts, to eradicate carriage) with treatment of active meningococcal disease, which instead requires an extended course of a bactericidal agent such as intravenous ceftriaxone.
concepts.original_wording: Source Pharma item 3 ("N. Meningitidis chemoprophylaxis ttt - Rifambin for 2 days"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Pharma item 3 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p3, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist
concepts.definition: Memantine is a moderate-affinity, uncompetitive (open-channel) NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. By blocking the pathological, low-level tonic activation of NMDA receptors that is thought to contribute to excitotoxic neuronal injury in Alzheimer disease, memantine is believed to be neuroprotective, while its lower affinity and rapid off-kinetics allow it to still permit the normal, high-amplitude physiological glutamate signalling needed for learning and memory. It is often used in combination with a cholinesterase inhibitor (such as donepezil), which acts through a different mechanism, for a modest additive symptomatic benefit.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify memantine's mechanism of action as NMDA receptor antagonism.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing memantine's mechanism (uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonism) with the cholinesterase inhibitors' mechanism (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine — increasing synaptic acetylcholine) — both drug classes are used in Alzheimer disease but act on entirely different neurotransmitter systems and are often combined rather than substituted for one another.
concepts.original_wording: Source Pharma item 4 ("Memantine - NMDA Receptor antagonistic"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Pharma item 4 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p3, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Riluzole's main mechanism of action in the treatment of ALS is presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channel blockade, reducing glutamate release
concepts.definition: Riluzole is used to modestly slow disease progression in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a disease in which excitotoxic glutamate signalling is believed to contribute to progressive motor neuron death. Its principal accepted mechanism is blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channels, which inhibits glutamate release from presynaptic terminals and dampens this excitotoxic drive; riluzole also has secondary effects on NMDA receptor-mediated responses. Unlike most other agents discussed in a general neuropharmacology course, riluzole does not reverse existing motor neuron loss or symptoms; its benefit is a modest extension of survival and time to ventilator dependence.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute riluzole's disease-modifying effect in ALS to presynaptic voltage-gated sodium channel blockade that reduces glutamate release.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Motor neuron disease pharmacology
concepts.pitfalls: Expecting riluzole to reverse weakness or restore lost motor neurons — its glutamate-reducing, sodium-channel-blocking mechanism only modestly slows disease progression and prolongs survival, it does not treat existing deficits.
concepts.original_wording: Source Pharma item 5 ("Riluzole main mechanism of action I'm ALS ttt - Sodium channel blocker"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Pharma item 5 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p3, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: CSF glucose level is unaltered (normal) in acute viral meningitis
concepts.definition: In acute viral (aseptic) meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically shows a lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis with a normal (unaltered) glucose level and a mildly elevated or normal protein, reflecting the absence of bacterial glucose consumption and the relatively intact blood-CSF barrier. This CSF glucose pattern is the key laboratory feature that distinguishes viral from bacterial meningitis, in which glucose is characteristically low because actively metabolising bacteria and recruited neutrophils consume glucose and CSF protein rises sharply from the acute inflammatory exudate. Because CSF findings overlap between viral meningitis and some other conditions (early bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis), clinical context and repeat sampling are used alongside glucose level when the picture is ambiguous.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that CSF glucose is normal (unaltered) in acute viral meningitis, contrasting with the low glucose of bacterial meningitis.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pathology > CNS infection CSF findings
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming CSF glucose is reduced in every type of meningitis — low glucose is a bacterial (and tuberculous/fungal) signature; viral meningitis characteristically spares CSF glucose, which is the discriminating laboratory feature between the two.
concepts.original_wording: Source Patho item 1 ("In ….. glucose level is unaltered - Acute viral meningitis"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Patho item 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p3, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Necrosis and microvascular proliferation are histologic hallmarks of glioblastoma (WHO grade 4)
concepts.definition: Glioblastoma, the WHO grade 4 (the highest-grade) diffuse astrocytic glioma, is histologically distinguished from lower-grade astrocytomas by two hallmark features: regions of tumour necrosis, classically with tumour cells arranged radially around the necrotic zone in a 'pseudopalisading' pattern, and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation, in which capillary endothelial and pericyte proliferation produces glomeruloid vascular tufts. Both features reflect the tumour's rapid growth outstripping its blood supply, triggering hypoxia-driven angiogenic signalling (notably via VEGF) and areas of tissue death. Their presence, even without the full range of anaplastic cytological features, is sufficient by itself to grade a diffuse astrocytoma as glioblastoma rather than a lower-grade lesion.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify necrosis and microvascular proliferation as the histologic hallmarks that grade a diffuse astrocytoma as glioblastoma (WHO grade 4).
concepts.pitfalls: Treating necrosis and microvascular proliferation as generic, non-specific tumour findings — in the WHO grading scheme for diffuse astrocytic gliomas, either feature alone is sufficient to upgrade a tumour to glioblastoma (grade 4), regardless of the degree of nuclear atypia present.
concepts.original_wording: Source Patho item 4 ("Necrosis/ microvascular proliferation - Glioblastoma ,grade 4"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Patho item 4 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p4, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: Astrocytes, part of the blood-brain barrier, are characterised by the intermediate filament GFAP
concepts.article_title: Astrocyte GFAP and the blood-brain barrier
concepts.definition: Astrocytes are the neuroglial cell type whose cytoskeleton is characteristically built on glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate filament specific to astrocytes and used histologically and immunohistochemically to identify them and tumours derived from them (e.g. astrocytomas). Astrocytic end-feet envelop the capillary endothelium of the central nervous system, and this astrocyte-endothelium relationship, together with the endothelial tight junctions themselves, is a key structural and functional component of the blood-brain barrier, which restricts and regulates the passage of substances between blood and brain tissue. Astrocytes also help maintain the extracellular ionic environment, provide metabolic support to neurons, and contribute to repair (gliosis) after CNS injury.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify astrocytes, marked by the intermediate filament GFAP, as the neuroglial cell type contributing to the blood-brain barrier.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Histology > Neuroglia and blood-brain barrier
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing GFAP (the astrocyte-specific intermediate filament) with other neuroglial or neuronal intermediate filaments — neurofilament proteins mark neurons, while GFAP specifically marks astrocytes, a distinction routinely used in neuropathology to identify a tumour's cell of origin.
concepts.original_wording: Source Histo item 1 ("Characteristic of neroglia sharing in BBB - Has Intermediate filament of GFAP"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as Histo item 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p6, answer/topic stated before the stem — this batch authors its own distractors.

concepts.label: The first pharyngeal arch's muscular derivatives are the four muscles of mastication plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric, all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
concepts.definition: The first pharyngeal (mandibular) arch gives rise to eight striated muscles: the four muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid) and four further muscles — tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and the anterior belly of digastric. Because muscles derived from a pharyngeal arch retain the nerve supply of that arch regardless of where they migrate to in the adult, all eight of these muscles are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), the first arch's nerve. This shared nerve supply is a reliable way to recall the full, otherwise unrelated-seeming, list of first-arch muscle derivatives.
concepts.explicit_objective: List the first pharyngeal arch's eight muscular derivatives and attribute their nerve supply to the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
concepts.pitfalls: Forgetting the four 'extra' first-arch muscles beyond the muscles of mastication (tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric) — all eight share mandibular (CN V3) nerve supply, the single fact that ties the otherwise scattered-looking list together.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q1 ("mention the muscultre derivatives of the first pharyngeal arch and their nerve supply"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p6.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p6, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha4beta2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, used for smoking cessation
concepts.definition: Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha4beta2 subtype of the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the principal receptor subtype mediating nicotine's rewarding, dopamine-releasing effect in the mesolimbic pathway. As a partial agonist, varenicline provides enough receptor stimulation to relieve nicotine craving and withdrawal symptoms, while its competitive occupancy of the receptor blocks nicotine from binding and producing its full rewarding effect if the patient smokes, blunting the reinforcement of relapse. Common adverse effects include nausea, vivid dreams, and a labelled risk of neuropsychiatric symptoms that warrants monitoring during a smoking-cessation course.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify varenicline's mechanism as alpha4beta2 nicotinic receptor partial agonism, used for smoking cessation.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating varenicline as either a pure agonist or a pure antagonist — its partial-agonist action is what lets it both relieve withdrawal (agonist component) and blunt the reward of smoking through the same receptor (competitive-blocking component).
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q2A part 1 ("..1..is α 4 β2 partial agonist for smoking cessation" → Varenicline), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p6-7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q2A part 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p6-7, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, used in the management of alcohol use disorder
concepts.definition: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, the enzyme that normally oxidises acetaldehyde (the first oxidation product of ethanol) to acetic acid. If a patient taking disulfiram drinks alcohol, acetaldehyde accumulates to toxic levels, producing an unpleasant disulfiram-ethanol reaction — flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, palpitations and hypotension — that is intended to deter further drinking as part of alcohol use disorder management. Because this reaction can be severe or even dangerous in patients with cardiac disease, disulfiram requires patient selection, informed consent, and avoidance of alcohol in any form, including some medications and foods that contain it.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute disulfiram's aversive effect in alcohol use disorder to inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase and consequent acetaldehyde accumulation.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Alcohol use disorder pharmacology
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing disulfiram's target (aldehyde dehydrogenase, the second enzyme in ethanol oxidation) with alcohol dehydrogenase (the first enzyme, which converts ethanol to acetaldehyde) — inhibiting the second enzyme is what causes acetaldehyde, rather than ethanol itself, to accumulate.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q2A part 2 ("….2… inhibit aldehyedehydrogenase enzyme, increases acetaldehyde , used for alcoholic management" → Disulfiram), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p6-7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q2A part 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p6-7, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Sodium bicarbonate is added to local anaesthetic solution to decrease its acidity and increase its activity
concepts.definition: Commercial local anaesthetic solutions are formulated at an acidic pH to keep the drug soluble and stable, but this leaves most of the anaesthetic molecules in their ionised (charged), poorly lipid-soluble form, which crosses the nerve sheath and axonal membrane slowly. Adding sodium bicarbonate raises the pH of the solution towards physiological, shifting more of the weak-base local anaesthetic into its unionised (uncharged), lipid-soluble form, which diffuses through the nerve membrane faster to reach its intracellular binding site on the voltage-gated sodium channel. The practical result of bicarbonate alkalinization is a faster onset of anaesthesia and less injection-site discomfort, without changing the eventual depth or duration of the block once equilibrium is reached.
concepts.explicit_objective: Explain how adding sodium bicarbonate to local anaesthetic solution decreases acidity and increases the drug's activity by favouring its unionised, lipid-soluble form.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming alkalinization changes the anaesthetic's ultimate efficacy or duration — it only speeds diffusion into the nerve by shifting the ionisation equilibrium, producing a faster onset rather than a stronger or longer block.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q2B part 1 ("….1.. added to local anesthesia to decrease acidity of ECF so increase its activity" → NaHCO3), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p7.

concepts.label: Infected or repeatedly inflamed tissue is more acidic, which reduces local anaesthetic activity
concepts.article_title: Tissue acidity and reduced local anaesthetic activity
concepts.definition: Infected or chronically inflamed tissue has a lower (more acidic) extracellular pH than healthy tissue, a consequence of local metabolic byproducts, hypoxia, and the inflammatory response. Because local anaesthetics are weak bases whose proportion of unionised, lipid-soluble drug depends on the surrounding pH relative to their pKa, this acidic extracellular environment shifts more of the drug into its ionised, poorly diffusible form, so less anaesthetic penetrates the nerve sheath to reach its site of action inside the axon. This is the pharmacological basis for the common clinical observation that local anaesthesia is less effective, or fails outright, when injected into an infected or abscessed area, sometimes requiring a regional nerve block placed outside the acidic field instead.
concepts.explicit_objective: Explain why infected or inflamed tissue's increased acidity reduces the activity of local anaesthetics injected into it.
aliases: Acidic tissue and local anaesthetic ionisation
concepts.pitfalls: Attributing local anaesthetic failure in infected tissue to inflammation-related vasodilation or drug washout alone — the ionisation-shift mechanism (more drug trapped in its charged form at low pH) is the pharmacologically primary explanation taught alongside any vascular contribution.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q2B part 2 ("….2…. increase ECF Acidity so decrease activity" → lidocaine HCL and repeated infections), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q2B part 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p7, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Imipramine is used, as a non-psychiatric indication, for nocturnal enuresis
concepts.definition: Imipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant, has a well-established non-psychiatric use in childhood nocturnal enuresis, historically one of the most common indications for prescribing it in paediatrics before behavioural and desmopressin-based approaches became first line. Its beneficial effect in enuresis is thought to combine its anticholinergic action (increasing bladder capacity, relaxing detrusor tone) with an effect on sleep architecture that reduces the depth of sleep during the hours the bladder would otherwise need to signal fullness. Because tricyclic antidepressants carry cardiotoxicity and overdose risk, particularly relevant in children, imipramine for enuresis is now generally reserved for cases refractory to first-line measures.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify imipramine's non-psychiatric use in the management of nocturnal enuresis.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Non-psychiatric uses of antidepressants
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming imipramine's benefit in enuresis is purely psychiatric or unrelated to its antidepressant identity — the same anticholinergic and sleep-architecture properties that cause side effects in depression treatment are what is exploited therapeutically in enuresis.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q3A part 1 ("Nocturnal enuresis- imipramine"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q3A part 1 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p7, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Duloxetine is used, as a non-psychiatric indication, for stress urinary incontinence
concepts.definition: Duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), has a non-psychiatric application in stress urinary incontinence, exploiting its action on the sacral spinal cord's Onuf's nucleus, whose motor neurons innervate the urethral striated sphincter. By increasing serotonin and norepinephrine availability at this nucleus, duloxetine enhances pudendal nerve motor output to the external urethral sphincter, increasing sphincter tone and closure pressure during episodes of raised abdominal pressure such as coughing or exertion. Duloxetine is also used for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia, indications that similarly depend on its combined serotonergic-noradrenergic reuptake inhibition rather than its antidepressant action per se.
concepts.explicit_objective: Identify duloxetine's non-psychiatric use in the management of stress urinary incontinence, via enhanced motor drive to the urethral sphincter.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Non-psychiatric uses of antidepressants
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming duloxetine relieves incontinence by a direct bladder or smooth-muscle action — its mechanism is central, acting on sacral motor neurons of the striated urethral sphincter via Onuf's nucleus, not a peripheral effect on the detrusor muscle.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q3A part 2 ("Urinary incontinence- duloxetine"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p7.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q3A part 2 of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p7, a short-answer fact with no printed options; the essay's third sub-fact (neuropathic pain — NDRI/TCA) named no specific drug and was folded into this fact's field notes rather than authored as a separate, under-specified item — this batch converts the retained facts to standard MCQs with its own distractors.

concepts.label: Valproate is not recommended for females of reproductive age because of teratogenicity and a PCOS-like syndrome of hirsutism and weight gain
concepts.definition: Valproate, a broad-spectrum antiepileptic and mood-stabilising drug, carries a well-documented set of adverse effects that disproportionately affect females of reproductive age: it is strongly teratogenic (associated with neural tube defects and a broader fetal valproate syndrome, among the highest-risk anticonvulsants in pregnancy) and is also associated with a polycystic-ovary-like endocrine syndrome, producing menstrual irregularities, hyperandrogenism-related hirsutism, and weight gain. Because of these risks, regulatory bodies and prescribing guidelines specifically restrict or require additional safeguards (pregnancy prevention programmes, specialist review) when valproate is prescribed to females of childbearing potential, favouring alternative antiepileptic or mood-stabilising agents where seizure or mood control allows.
concepts.explicit_objective: State the reasons valproate is not recommended for females of reproductive age: teratogenicity and a PCOS-like syndrome of hirsutism/weight gain.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Antiepileptic adverse effects in females
concepts.pitfalls: Attributing valproate's female-specific caution to teratogenicity alone — the drug also has an independent, non-pregnancy-related endocrine liability (a PCOS-like syndrome), which is a separate reason for caution even outside pregnancy planning.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q3B part 1 ("GIVE RESEON Why Valproate and phenytoin are not recommended for Females - valprote cause polycyctic ovaries / hair loss / increase body weight"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p8.

concepts.label: Phenytoin is not recommended for females of reproductive age because of hirsutism, acne and gingival hyperplasia
concepts.definition: Phenytoin, a sodium-channel-blocking antiepileptic, produces a characteristic set of cosmetic adverse effects that make it particularly poorly tolerated by female patients: gingival hyperplasia (overgrowth of the gums, worsened by poor oral hygiene), coarsening of facial features, acne, and hirsutism. These effects arise from phenytoin's actions on connective tissue and androgen-related pathways rather than from its anticonvulsant mechanism itself, and they are dose- and duration-dependent, often becoming more noticeable with prolonged therapy. Because of this cosmetic burden, alongside its own teratogenic risk (fetal hydantoin syndrome) and complex pharmacokinetics, phenytoin is often avoided in favour of newer antiepileptics when treating females of reproductive age.
concepts.explicit_objective: State the reasons phenytoin is not recommended for females of reproductive age: gingival hyperplasia, acne and hirsutism.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Pharmacology > Antiepileptic adverse effects in females
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing phenytoin's cosmetic adverse-effect profile (gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, acne, coarse facies) with valproate's distinct one (PCOS-like syndrome, weight gain) — the two antiepileptics are both discouraged in females of reproductive age but for different constellations of adverse effects.

concepts.label: Motivation is the force that activates or inhibits behaviour to achieve a goal
concepts.definition: Motivation is defined physiologically and behaviourally as the internal force, or set of processes, that activates, directs and sustains goal-directed behaviour, and that can equally inhibit behaviours that do not serve the current goal. It integrates internal drive states (such as hunger, thirst, or an emotional state) with external incentives (the perceived value of a goal) to determine whether, how vigorously, and in what direction an organism acts. Motivation is closely tied to the brain's reward circuitry, since the anticipated or received reward value of an outcome is a principal factor shaping how strongly a given behaviour is activated or inhibited.
concepts.explicit_objective: State the definition of motivation as the force that activates or inhibits behaviour to achieve a goal.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Motivation and limbic system
concepts.pitfalls: Treating motivation as purely an internal drive state — the definition explicitly includes its role in both activating and inhibiting behaviour, and integrates external incentive value together with internal drive.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q4 part A ("Define motivation… Motivation : the force that activate or inhibit certain behavior to achieve certain goal"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p8.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as essay Q4 part A of EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf (src_b67868be37571f92a53f), p8, a short-answer fact with no printed options — this batch converts it to a standard MCQ with its own distractors.

concepts.label: The limbic lobe mediates the reward and punishment systems underlying motivated behaviour
concepts.article_title: Limbic lobe reward and punishment systems
concepts.definition: The limbic lobe (encompassing the cingulate gyrus, hippocampal formation, amygdala, septal area, and their connections to the hypothalamus and midbrain) mediates two functionally opposed systems that shape motivated behaviour: a reward (approach) system, centred on the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and septal region, which reinforces behaviours associated with pleasurable or beneficial outcomes, and a punishment (aversion) system, involving structures such as the amygdala and periventricular regions, which discourages behaviours associated with pain or threat. The balance of activity between these reward and punishment circuits, both anatomically part of the limbic lobe, is what allows an organism to approach beneficial stimuli and avoid harmful ones, underlying the limbic lobe's broader role in emotion and motivation.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute reward (approach) and punishment (aversion) behavioural systems to the limbic lobe.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Physiology > Motivation and limbic system
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the reward and punishment systems as a single undifferentiated limbic function — they are anatomically and neurochemically distinguishable circuits (dopaminergic mesolimbic reward pathway versus amygdala-centred aversion circuitry) that happen to share a common limbic-lobe home.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q4 part B ("illustrate limbic lobe role… Reward and punishment system… main neurotransmitter"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p8.

concepts.label: Lithium toxicity is managed by stopping lithium, increasing fluid intake and diuresis (avoiding diuretics that reduce lithium clearance), and haemodialysis in severe cases
concepts.definition: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, and toxicity, precipitated by dehydration, renal impairment, or interacting drugs, produces a spectrum from tremor and gastrointestinal upset to confusion, seizures and coma. Management begins with immediately stopping lithium and increasing fluid intake to promote renal clearance, since lithium is excreted almost entirely unchanged by the kidney and is reabsorbed alongside sodium in the proximal tubule; diuretics that promote sodium loss, particularly thiazides, must specifically be avoided because they paradoxically increase proximal lithium reabsorption and worsen toxicity. In severe toxicity (very high levels, significant neurological symptoms, or renal failure preventing adequate clearance), haemodialysis is used to remove lithium directly, since it is small and not protein-bound and dialyses efficiently.
concepts.explicit_objective: Outline the management of lithium toxicity: stopping lithium, increasing fluid intake, diuresis while avoiding lithium-retaining diuretics, and haemodialysis for severe cases.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming any diuretic helps clear lithium — thiazide diuretics specifically worsen lithium retention by increasing proximal tubular reabsorption, so the diuresis used in management must avoid this class.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q5 part A ("How to manage Li toxicity? … stop Li, increse Fluid intake, diuresis (avoid diuretics), and Hemodilysis"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p8.

concepts.label: Atypical antipsychotics have less extrapyramidal side effects and more efficacy against negative symptoms than typical antipsychotics
concepts.article_title: Advantages of atypical over typical antipsychotics
concepts.definition: Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics act predominantly through high-affinity D2 dopamine receptor antagonism, which effectively controls positive symptoms of schizophrenia but, by strongly blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway, produces prominent extrapyramidal side effects (parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia) and provides little benefit for negative symptoms. Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotics combine lower or more transient D2 antagonism with serotonin 5-HT2A antagonism, a combination that produces fewer extrapyramidal side effects at therapeutic doses and, through this same serotonin-dopamine interaction, more meaningful efficacy against the negative symptoms of schizophrenia (flat affect, avolition, social withdrawal) than typical agents achieve. These two advantages, together with a generally lower risk of tardive dyskinesia, are the principal reasons atypical antipsychotics are now preferred as first-line therapy in most guidelines, despite their own distinct risk of metabolic side effects.
concepts.explicit_objective: State two advantages of atypical over typical antipsychotics: fewer extrapyramidal side effects and greater efficacy against negative symptoms.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming atypical antipsychotics are free of significant adverse effects because they cause fewer extrapyramidal symptoms — their advantage is specifically in the EPS and negative-symptom domains, while they carry their own distinct liability for metabolic side effects (weight gain, dyslipidaemia, new-onset diabetes).
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q5 part B ("Avantages of Atypical over typical… Less pyramidal side effect… More efficacy (in – ve symptoms)"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p9.

concepts.label: The anterior cerebral artery's central (perforating) branches supply the anterior caudate and lentiform nuclei and the genu and inferior anterior limb of the internal capsule
concepts.definition: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA), proximal to and around the anterior communicating artery, gives off small anteromedial central (perforating) branches that pierce the anterior perforated substance to supply deep structures near the midline: the anterior parts of the caudate nucleus and the lentiform (lenticular) nucleus, and the genu together with the lower (inferior) half of the anterior limb of the internal capsule. The largest and most clinically significant of these perforators is the recurrent artery of Heubner, whose occlusion classically produces contralateral weakness of the face and arm from internal capsule involvement, sometimes with subtle personality or behavioural change from caudate involvement. These central branches are functionally and clinically distinct from the ACA's cortical branches, which instead supply the medial and superomedial surface of the cerebral hemisphere.
concepts.explicit_objective: Attribute supply of the anterior caudate/lentiform nuclei and the genu/inferior anterior limb of the internal capsule to the anterior cerebral artery's central (perforating) branches.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Anterior cerebral artery central branches
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the ACA's central (perforating) branches, which supply deep basal ganglia/internal capsule structures, with its cortical branches, which supply the medial hemispheric surface — the two branch groups have entirely different territories and different clinical stroke syndromes.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q6 part A ("mention the distribution of anterior cerebral artery… Central: Anteromedial set: peirce the ant perforated substance to supply the ant part of cudate and lentiform + internal capsule (genu and lower half of ant limb)"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p9.

concepts.label: The anterior cerebral artery's cortical branches supply the medial hemispheric surface (except the occipital lobe), a strip of the superolateral surface, and part of the orbital surface
concepts.definition: The anterior cerebral artery's cortical branches supply almost the entire medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere from the frontal to the parietal lobe, sparing only the occipital lobe, which is instead supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. These branches also wrap over the superomedial margin to supply a roughly one-inch-wide strip of the adjoining superolateral (convexity) surface, and supply part of the orbital (inferior frontal) surface via the medial orbital branches. This territory explains the classic clinical picture of an ACA infarct: contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss (from the medial surface's leg/foot motor and sensory homunculus), sparing the face and hand, which lie in the middle cerebral artery's lateral convexity territory instead.
concepts.explicit_objective: Describe the anterior cerebral artery's cortical territory: the medial hemispheric surface except the occipital lobe, a superolateral strip, and part of the orbital surface.
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Anterior cerebral artery cortical territory
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the ACA supplies the entire medial surface without exception — the occipital lobe's medial surface belongs to the posterior cerebral artery, a boundary that matters for localising infarcts and for understanding why ACA strokes spare vision.
concepts.original_wording: Source essay Q6 part B ("Cortical: Medial surface (except occipital lobe), Letral surface (one inch strip sup.), Inferior surface (medial part of orbital surface)"), short-answer format, read from EOM - CNS final paper 2 2024.pdf, p9.
